bullets: ‘a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner!’: **asyndetic list** of grasping verbs; ‘sinner’ adds religious condemnation.
‘Hard and sharp as flint… secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster’: **similes** of hardness and isolation; polysyndeton emphasises his closed nature.
‘The cold within him froze his old features’: **pathetic fallacy reversed**: the cold comes from inside him.
‘Bah! Humbug!’: dismissal of Christmas.
‘Are there no prisons?’ … ‘decrease the surplus population’: voices Poor Law and Malthusian views.
He keeps Bob’s fire to ‘one coal’ and lives alone in gloomy rooms: meanness even to himself.
core.p: Scrooge is introduced as the embodiment of greed and coldness.

bullets: ‘a solitary child, neglected by his friends’: sympathy; explains his coldness.
He weeps and wishes he had given something to a carol singer: first sign of change.
Fezziwig’s ball shows he once valued kindness; he admits Fezziwig’s power to make people ‘happy or unhappy’.
Belle: ‘Another idol has displaced me… a golden one’: money replaced love.
core.h: Stave 2: the boy and the young man
core.p: The past reveals Scrooge as a neglected child who once loved and was loved.

bullets: He asks ‘with an interest he had never felt before’ whether Tiny Tim will live: **compassion** awakens.
His own words about ‘surplus population’ are thrown back at him; he is ‘overcome with penitence and grief’.
He enjoys Fred’s party games, ‘as eager as a boy’.
core.p: Scrooge becomes a humble learner, increasingly emotionally involved.

bullets: ‘I fear you more than any spectre I have seen’: the silent future terrifies him.
At the grave: ‘Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of things that May be, only?’: hope of change.
‘I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future.’
core.p: Facing death, Scrooge fears what he has become.

bullets: ‘I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a school-boy. I am as giddy as a drunken man.’: **anaphora** and **similes** of lightness and childlike joy.
Sends a turkey to the Cratchits; gives a huge donation; joins Fred’s party; raises Bob’s salary.
‘He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew’: **tricolon**; reintegration into society.
‘to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father’.

callouts.p: Scrooge represents the selfish, wealthy Victorian middle class. His redemption shows Dickens’s belief that such people can change, and that change begins with empathy.

core.p: Scrooge becomes joyful, generous and connected.

model: Stave 1 coldness and views on the poor
Stave 3 compassion for Tiny Tim; his words thrown back
Context: Dickens’s purpose to reform middle-class attitudes
exam.q: Explain how Scrooge changes elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Track the change with one quotation per stave.

mistakes.r: His change is gradual from Stave 2 onwards.
Stave 2 shows the causes of his coldness and invites sympathy.

quotes.a: Isolated and closed, but with hidden potential (pearl).

quotes.q: The cold within him froze his old features

quotes.a: Money worshipped as a false god.

quotes.q: I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future

quotes.a: Free from the chains of greed.
Takes social responsibility for the poor.

summary: Scrooge is the protagonist whose transformation from a cold, isolated miser to a generous ‘second father’ carries Dickens’s message: learn how he is presented in each stave, the key quotations, and what he represents.

terms.d: Being saved from sin through repentance.
